title: Train or test first? Splitting a tiny dataset without fooling yourself
scenario: You have 800 labeled customer reviews and want to train a sentiment classifier. A teammate says: train on all 800, then check accuracy on the same 800. Another says: split 80/20 first, train on 640, test on 160. Explain which approach is honest, why testing on training data lies, and what goes wrong when the test set leaks into decisions (like tuning on it repeatedly).

rubric.point: Says to split before training and evaluate on held-out data the model never saw
Explains that testing on training data overstates accuracy because the model memorized those rows
Mentions that repeatedly tuning on the same test set leaks information and a separate validation split or cross-validation fixes it
Notes the split should preserve class balance (stratify) or at least be random, not first-640 vs last-160
Gives a concrete check, e.g. compare train vs test accuracy and expect test to be lower

explanation: Always split BEFORE training: fit on the train slice, measure once on the held-out test slice. Accuracy on training rows is memorization, not learning, so it reads too high. If you tune hyperparameters against the same test set over and over, the test set quietly becomes training data — keep a separate validation split (or cross-validate) and touch the final test set once. Split randomly and stratify by label so both slices have the same class mix; a large train/test gap is the smell of overfitting.

title: Accuracy says 98% but the model catches nothing
scenario: A fraud team has 10,000 transactions, only 150 are fraud. A junior ships a model with 98.5% accuracy that predicts 'not fraud' for everything, catching zero fraud cases. Explain why accuracy lies here, which two metrics you would report instead, and what one-line baseline every fraud model must beat.

rubric.point: Identifies the class imbalance (150/10000) and that predicting the majority class gives fake high accuracy
Names precision and recall (or F1) as the honest metrics for the rare class
States the trivial baseline: a model that always predicts not-fraud scores ~98.5%, so any real model must beat that on recall
Explains the tradeoff: catching more fraud (recall) usually costs more false alarms (precision)
Proposes a concrete fix direction, e.g. threshold tuning, class weights, or resampling

explanation: With 1.5% fraud, 'always predict legit' scores 98.5% accuracy while catching nothing — accuracy measures the majority class here. Report precision (of flagged transactions, how many are real fraud) and recall (of real fraud, how much you catch), or F1 to combine them. Any model must beat the do-nothing baseline on recall, not accuracy. Then trade precision against recall with the decision threshold, class weights, or resampling — there is no free lunch, only the tradeoff the business prefers.

title: The model memorized the training set and flopped on new customers
scenario: A churn model hits 99% accuracy on training data but 71% on new customers. The model is a deep decision tree with no depth limit and 200 features for 2,000 rows. Name the problem, explain why the train/test gap is the diagnosis, and list two specific fixes you would try first.

rubric.point: Names overfitting: the model memorized training noise instead of learning general patterns
Explains the train/test gap (99% vs 71%) as the signature symptom of overfitting
Proposes limiting model capacity, e.g. max depth, min samples per leaf, or pruning
Proposes a second fix: fewer/better features, more data, regularization, or cross-validation
Says how to confirm the fix worked: gap shrinks and test accuracy rises on unseen data

explanation: This is textbook overfitting: unlimited tree depth plus 200 features on 2,000 rows lets the model memorize. The 28-point train/test gap is the diagnosis — a healthy model has a small gap. First fixes: cap capacity (max_depth, min_samples_leaf) and validate with cross-validation; then cut weak features, add data, or regularize. You know it worked when the gap shrinks AND held-out accuracy goes up — train accuracy alone dropping means nothing.

title: The model looks great in staging, terrible on Monday mornings
scenario: You built a churn model for a telecom app. Offline AUC is 0.91. In production, every Monday morning between 6 and 9 the app serves a suspended feature flag and traffic drops 70%. Last quarter, live AUC on served predictions is 0.72, and the gap grows each week. The data pipeline pulls features from the app's production database: some features are computed **after** the churn decision is made (e.g. `days_since_final_push_notification`, `csat_after_agent_call`). Retraining weekly does not close the gap. Debug this: list the likely causes you would check first, how you would confirm each one, and what you would change.

rubric.point: Identifies label or feature leakage from post-decision features (features computed after the churn event) as a likely cause
Identifies train-serving skew: features computed differently offline vs online, or missing/timeout features online filled with defaults
Proposes a concrete way to confirm each cause, e.g. comparing offline vs online feature distributions, backfilling historical features chronologically, or shadow scoring
Notes the Monday traffic/feature pattern as a distribution-shift or data-availability signal worth correlating with the degradation
Mentions time-based train/val split or point-in-time correct joins as part of the retraining fix

explanation: Three separate problems are stacked here. (1) **Leakage**: features like `days_since_final_push_notification` are computed after the label window ends, so they encode the outcome. Drop them or compute them point-in-time. (2) **Train-serving skew**: features joined from a production DB at serve time need to match exactly what was available at training time; the standard fix is a feature store or point-in-time correct historical snapshots. (3) **Distribution shift**: the Monday pattern (low traffic, suspended flags) changes the feature distribution, and staleness grows week to week. Confirm with distribution comparisons, chronological backtests and shadow scoring. Weekly retraining cannot fix leakage or skew because both survive retraining.

title: Passenger forecast never fails loudly, it just drifts to useless
scenario: A transit agency predicts hourly passenger flow to staff counters. The pipeline recomputes predictions hourly and has run for 18 months. Accuracy dashboards show MAPE creeping from 8% to 22% over the year. Nobody changed the model. Inputs include weather (an external API), calendar, and lagged counts. There is also a single Super Bowl rerun incident; a holiday calendar change went in last March and half the new holiday dates were wrong for the first 3 weeks. Explain the sources of the creep you would prioritize, and how you would separate model aging from data-quality causes from truly-irreducible drift.

rubric.point: Frames slow MAPE creep as concept drift or covariate drift, and distinguishes the two
Flags the external weather API as a drift/silent-failure vector (schema changes, unit changes, stale cache, wrong values served)
Names the holiday calendar corruption as a data-quality incident that must be segmented out before blame is assigned to the model
References rolling retraining windows or scheduled recalibration as the standard response to gradual drift
Proposes monitoring inputs and residual slices over time rather than a single MAPE line, to localize where accuracy is lost

explanation: Gradual degradation with no model change almost always means either (a) concept drift (the world changed: ridership patterns post-event), (b) covariate shift (the input distributions moved: weather API changes, calendar changes), or (c) silent data breakage, which Incident A is a hint for. Wrong holiday dates for three weeks is data quality, not drift; it must be isolated (time-bounded residual spike). The correct posture is slice-wise monitoring (by hour, holiday flag, weather bucket), drift detectors on inputs, and rolling retraining or recalibration with a validation window that matches serving conditions. One global MAPE number cannot distinguish any of these causes.

title: Fraud model saves money on paper, detects nobody in practice
scenario: A payments team trains a fraud classifier on 2.1M historical transactions. Fraud rate is 0.4%. They train on the raw data, split randomly into train/test, and report recall 34% and precision 62% on the held-out set. In a two-week live shadow trial the model caught 5 of 40 confirmed fraud cases, and 3 of those 5 were also caught by the old rule engine. Precision did hold up. What went wrong between the offline report and the shadow trial? Be specific about the split and about any metric claims you would not trust.

rubric.point: Identifies random splitting of temporal transaction data as the core flaw (leakage across time / train-serving mismatch)
Explains that a chronological (time-based) split is required so the test set looks like the future
Notes that fraud patterns drift, so an old test period can be easier and inflate recall
Avoids over-trusting a single aggregate recall: proposes stratified or cost-based metrics (precision-recall curves, catch-rate at fixed review budget)
Respects the 0.4% base rate: recognizes that 'precision 62%' on a small, randomly-sampled test slice can be misleading without volume context

explanation: A random split over a time-ordered transaction stream lets the model see 'tomorrow' during training: autocorrelated fraud rings, repeated customers, and leaked aggregates survive the split. After the split, the test no longer represents the deployment task (score the future), so recall is inflated. Fraud patterns also shift month to month, so a stale hold-out is easy. The right evaluation uses a chronological split (train on the past, test on the future) or rolling-origin evaluation, with metrics reported at operationally meaningful thresholds (e.g. catch rate under a fixed reviewer budget), plus confidence intervals because 40 confirmations is a tiny sample.

title: The recommendation pipeline runs 40 minutes late every night and nobody noticed for a month
scenario: An e-tenant recommendation batch job has a hard SLA of 01:00. On three separate occasions, the upstream order ingest hiccupped; retries were forced; the job then succeeded at 01:40 for two weeks straight. Every report replies on the recommendations from 01:40 until the next correct run. No alert fired. Design the monitoring that would have caught this in the first day, without adding a second heavy job. Also say what you would do about the three two-week periods where served recommendations were stale.

rubric.point: Proposes a freshness check: alert if the recommendation table's write timestamp has not advanced by the expected time (SLA + margin)
Proposes a data-volume / row-count check rather than job success alone, since 'success' on partial output is silent failure
Separates job success from data correctness: monitors both, and alerts on late-success specifically
Proposes that the consumer side detect stale recommendations (serving reads a manifest or minimum-version) rather than serving whatever is present
For retrograde handling: label the stale period, note the analysis is still useful, and add a backfill or versioned manifest so analysis can exclude that period

explanation: This is the classic silent-failure shape: the job pages 'green', the data is served anyway, and both the producer and the consumer assume the other is checking. The fix needs no second job. It needs three cheap checks: (1) freshness — the recommendation manifest version or last-written timestamp must advance by the SLA plus a margin; (2) volume — row counts (or hashes of key windows) must be in the expected band; (3) late-success alerting — the job completing at 01:40 is itself an SLA breach to alert on. On the consumer side, serve only from a versioned manifest; if the version does not roll over, stop serving or serve a fallback with a visible banner. For the historical two-week periods: annotate them, and prefer time-partitioned output so affected windows can be re-analyzed or excluded rather than silently blended.

title: Anomaly detector that flags the same zones for three years
scenario: A city water utility has a leak-detection pipeline. Every night it computes per-zone flow signatures; an ML anomaly detector ranks 'most unusual zones'. Ops teams have complained for a year that the same 12 zones appear weekly, and after inspection about a third of them are structural facts of those zones (an old district meter, a fountain, a school). Zone A is a fountain that is unusual every summer and treated as a leak each time. When a real leak appeared (burst main), it ranked 7th, below the known recurring zones. Diagnose why recurrence crowds out true novelty, and propose a fix that preserves the strength of the anomaly detector without annoying ops into ignoring it.

rubric.point: Identifies that recurring 'anomalies' are unusual-but-known zones, i.e. the detector never models seasonality or long-running normal-unusual patterns
Explains that novelty should be judged relative to a baseline for that zone and time of year/context, not globally
Proposes suppressing or down-weighting known-recurring zones via per-zone baselines, feedback from ops dispositions, or persistence/suppression lists
Distinguishes detection score magnitude from rank; explains the burst main ranked low because known zones soak up the score
Proposes an evaluation for alerts that includes operator feedback (lack of fatigue, precision@k, time-to-detect) rather than a fixed score cutoff

explanation: The detector learned to score 'how unusual is this zone overall' and surprise is persistent in a place, tools like an old district meter are always a bit weird. That is a seasonality and per-zone baseline problem: an anomaly must be measured against what that zone does in July, not what all zones do on average year-round. Once ops dispositions are captured, you can learn a per-zone (and per-season) baseline and suppress or down-rank known recurring signatures. Rank is what people act on; do not let persistent quick wins (recurring zones) crowd out genuine novelty — reserve some budget for 'different from its own history'. Evaluate the detector on usefulness to ops: precision at review capacity, novelty share of true positives, and declining time-to-detect, rather than a raw score threshold.

title: Tests pass, model 'improves', nightly batch quietly eats the future
scenario: A team ships a nightly-retrained demand model. Code review was clean and unit tests pass. A sharp reviewer notices the feature engineering builds a `dow_week_hour_mean_of_orders` variable using the **entire** order table, including the day being predicted, and reference to two days after the split in a leaky rolling window. Offline MAE improved 4% when this feature was added. Nobody in the room can say whether the improvement is real. What do you do before the next deploy, in what order, and what change to the test suite prevents recurrence?

rubric.point: Names the bug: aggregates computed over data that includes the prediction target window leak the future
Says the 4% offline gain cannot be trusted until re-evaluated with point-in-time correct features
Blocks the deploy (freezes the change) and re-runs evaluation with a chronological split before comparing
Proposes a pipeline-level test that checks for temporal leakage, e.g. asserting no used feature is computed from data after the cutoff for each row
Notes that leakage shows up as too-good gains on aggregates that fail to reproduce on truly unseen time slices

explanation: Aggregating over the full table including rows after the prediction cutoff is textbook leakage: the 'improvement' is the model reading the answer. You cannot quantify the true effect without re-evaluating with point-in-time correct features on a chronological split — the current 4% is not evidence of anything except leakage. Concretely: freeze the change (do not deploy), rewrite the aggregator to be cutoff-aware (a running/expanding or pre-cutoff-window aggregate for each historical row), re-run the same evaluation, and only then compare. Long-term: add a leak test to the suite that asserts for every feature the data used is strictly before each row's cutoff, and a date-line invariant ('the model at time T never sees any row with timestamp > T'). Tests passing means nothing here because nothing in the unit suite verifies point-in-time correctness — that invariant must be encoded.
